Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (799 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that an independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity.
  • Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image indicates the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away.
  • The image of this black hole, designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that an independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity, which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like.

Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image indicates the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away.

The image of this black hole, designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all?

Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky.

"It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai mentioned in a statement sent to Space.com via email.

Sources indicate that lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an key step in the scientific process.".

This could settle the questions of just how the final image of M87* was influenced by both atmospheric effects and the processing methods needed to reconstruct pictures from telescope data.

That's not just good news for the EHT; it's good news for Einstein.

Einstein published his theory of general relativity in 1915, completely reshaping how we think of gravity. General relativity suggested that objects with mass curve the very fabric of space and time, united as a single entity called spacetime. Gravity arises from that curvature.

The greater the mass, the more extreme the curvature and thus the greater the gravitational influence of that object. Taking this to its extreme, scientist Karl Schwarzschild came up with a solution to the equations of general relativity that suggested an infinitesimal region with infinite mass, resulting in unrestrained curvature, a singularity. Around this would be a spherical boundary at which not even light has the velocity needed to escape this region. Referred to as the Schwarzschild radius, that boundary became known as the event horizon of a black hole. The singularity, its heart. Black holes were born in 1915, decades before their discovery and over a century before the EHT saw one.

General relativity also predicted what the region around the event horizon would look like. A ring of superheated glowing plasma with the shadow of the black hole falling on it.When scientists first saw the image of M87* they were astounded at how close it reflected predictions made by general relativity, thus confirming the the theory once again. This verification further solidifies that development.

Verifying the EHT's image of M87* could lead to the CSIRO-developed technique being applied to some more "down-to-Earth" uses such as improving medical imaging and mapping earthquakes.

Sources indicate that "Independent validation is at the heart of the scientific process, and it is especially valuable for results as novel as those of the EHT. It is extremely gratifying to see that GenDIReCT, an elegant, entirely independent method, recovers the ring structure of M87* across several years, in excellent agreement with the EHT Collaboration’s published results," Laurent Loinard, Director of the EHT Collaboration, said.

"Studies like this strengthen our confidence in what we have learned about black holes, and enrich the toolkit available to the whole community.".

Industry observers note that the team's research was published on Wednesday (Nov. 11) in the journal Nature.

Robert Lea is a science journalist in the U.K. whose articles have been published in Physics World, Fresh Scientist, Astronomy Magazine, All About Space, Newsweek and ZME Science. He also writes about science communication for Elsevier and the European Journal of Physics. Rob holds a bachelor of science degree in physics and astronomy from the U.K.’s Open University. #36311. Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Hidden ecosystem: Scientists discover 245 animals living inside a single deep-sea rock

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1087 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form.
  • Sources indicate that although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean.
  • It has been revealed that polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that deep beneath the Pacific Ocean, scientists have uncovered a surprising world of tiny animals living inside metal-rich rocks that take millions of years to form. These rocks, known as polymetallic nodules, contain miniature cracks and cavities that provide shelter for creatures smaller than a millimeter.

Sources indicate that although they may look like ordinary stones, these nodules offer something unusual in the deep ocean. They create hard surfaces in an environment dominated by soft mud, while their internal spaces provide additional habitats for marine life.

It has been revealed that polymetallic nodules are dark, roughly fist-sized formations made largely of iron and manganese oxides. They grow at an extraordinarily slow pace, often adding only a few millimeters over a million years. Found at ocean depths ranging from 4,000 to 6,000 meters, they can remain on the seafloor for millions of years.

Researchers set out to investigate the tiny organisms living within these ancient formations and determine how important the nodules are to deep-sea biodiversity.

Dr. Tanja Stratmann, a deep-sea ecologist and one of the study's three lead authors, explains: "In our study we show that the sizes of cracks inside the nodules are large enough to provide home to animals that are smaller than a millimeter in size.".

Hundreds of Tiny Animals Found Inside a Single Rock.

Industry observers note that to explore these hidden habitats, the research team collected nodules from the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, a vast region of the central Pacific Ocean. They used specialized sampling equipment, including box corers that collect sections of the seafloor and remotely operated diving robots capable of working at extreme depths.

Back in the laboratory, the researchers carefully opened the nodules and extracted the tiny animals concealed within their cracks and crevices.

The results revealed an unexpectedly rich community of marine life. Across 244 nodules, the team identified 4,139 individual animals. Each nodule contained an average of 17 animals, but one particularly crowded specimen sheltered an astonishing 245 individuals.

Industry observers note that the discovery indicates that these rocks are more than simple surfaces where marine organisms can attach themselves. Their intricate internal structures create three-dimensional living spaces, allowing animals to inhabit protected areas within the nodules themselves.

Dr. Coral Diaz-Recio Lorenzo explains: "The crevices in the polymetallic nodules function as small shelters and provide home to animals that we do not encounter in the soft sediment of the seafloor.".

Hidden Ecosystems Unlike Those on the Surrounding Seafloor.

Although the nodules contained fewer animals than the surrounding muddy sediment, their contribution to deep-sea life was still substantial.

Recent findings suggest that for roundworms (nematodes), the number living inside the nodules amounted to approximately 10% of the number found in the surrounding sediment. For tiny crustaceans (copepods), the figure was about 25%.

However, the most key finding was not simply how many animals the researchers discovered. It was how different the communities inside the rocks were from those living in the nearby mud.

Genetic analyses revealed that the animals inhabiting the nodules formed distinctive communities. Remarkably, these communities remained highly similar across locations separated by large distances (up to 1,000 km), even though they differed significantly from the organisms found in the surrounding seafloor sediment.

Sources indicate that this suggests that polymetallic nodules support specialized habitats that are not easily replaced by other parts of the deep ocean. Their cracks and cavities offer living conditions that certain organisms appear to depend on.

Deep-Sea Mining Could Destroy These Ancient Habitats.

The findings raise serious concerns about the potential environmental consequences of deep-sea mining.

According to recent reports, polymetallic nodules contain economically valuable metals, including nickel, cobalt, and copper. These resources have attracted interest in industrial mining operations that would collect the nodules directly from the ocean floor.

However, removing the rocks would also eliminate the miniature habitats they contain, along with the animals living inside them.

Sources indicate that one example is Thurammina sp. 1, a single-celled organism found particularly frequently within the nodules. This species appears especially well adapted to the sheltered spaces inside the rocks, making it an example of the specialized life that could be threatened by their removal.

Sources indicate that the problem is that these habitats cannot quickly recover. Because polymetallic nodules require millions of years to develop, latest ones would not form within a human lifetime. Mining could therefore eliminate ecosystems that would take geological timescales to replace.

Prof. Sabine Gollner warns: "Our findings point out that commercial mining may result in an irreversible loss of undescribed and unique biodiversity associated to nodules. This needs to be considered in environmental management of deep-sea mining.".

Scientists Race to Understand What Could Be Lost.

Sources indicate that the discovery highlights an often overlooked aspect of ocean conservation. Protecting deep-sea ecosystems requires more than safeguarding large, visible animals. It also means considering the microscopic and nearly microscopic organisms that inhabit specialized environments hidden within the seafloor.

An important question remains unanswered: If deep-sea mining destroys these nodule communities, could some species disappear entirely?

Recent findings suggest that researchers still need to determine whether organisms that depend on the nodules also inhabit other parts of the ocean. If certain species are restricted to these habitats, removing the nodules could potentially contribute to their global extinction.

Understanding where these animals live and how widely they are distributed will be essential for identifying areas that need protection and evaluating the potential ecological damage caused by deep-sea mining.

To investigate further, Dr. Tanja Stratmann is currently participating in an international research expedition to the Clarion-Clipperton Zone, where scientists are continuing to study the ecosystems associated with polymetallic nodules.

This expedition and other follow-up investigations are independently funded through the JPIOcean projects MiningImpact 2 and 3.

The findings reveal that even a single rock on the deep ocean floor can support a surprisingly complex community of life. As interest in harvesting the ocean's mineral resources grows, scientists are working to understand these hidden ecosystems before habitats that took millions of years to form are permanently lost.

#36310. ‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2525 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nature ↗ Open Full Page

‘I had felt overconfident’: senior scientists reveal mistakes that aided discovery

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2525 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did.
  • To err is human, science endeavours included.
  • Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicist Peter Shawhan and his team perfected not finding gravitational waves at the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) facility in Livingston, Louisiana — until they did. Credit: Igor Andreoni/Peter Shawhan.

To err is human, science endeavours included. Accounts of missteps in the laboratory or field abound among early-career researchers, as do tales of what they learnt from them. But senior scientists make mistakes, too — and not just early in their careers.

Sometimes, reaching a dead end was the only way around a problem. Other times, graduate students saved their advisers from throwing away ‘wrong’ data. Senior scientists also know the dangers of overthinking and how it can lead to experimental paralysis. “Every year, I devote a meeting with students and postdocs to discuss failures and how errors of judgement or methods are part of academic life,” notes Catherine Badgley, a palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. “I hope this helps them to see they can learn from mistakes rather than be devastated by them.”.

Nature’s careers team spoke to Badgley and four other senior scientists to hear about their ‘failures’ and the lessons they took from them.

Physicist at the University of Maryland in College Park and a deputy spokesperson for the Laser Interferometer Gravitational Wave Observatory (LIGO) scientific collaboration.

According to recent reports, for the past 26 years, I have been searching for gravitational waves with LIGO, which has a gravitational-wave observatory in Livingston, Louisiana. These waves are echoes of massive events such as the merging of black holes or the collision of neutron stars. They produce ripples in space-time and, by the time these tiny ripples reach Earth, they are so faint that scientists need extra help to ‘hear’ them, because they are extremely hard to detect by just using light, or telescopes, to see them. For example, observations of a collision of two neutron stars with telescopes has revealed the presence of gold and platinum atoms, solving a long-standing question: what is the origin of about half of all elements heavier than iron? The detection of such an event with LIGO would get us even more information.

It has been revealed that in the first tests of LIGO, the team found nothing. Later, with improved detectors, we still found nothing.

It has been revealed that in fact, we got very good at reporting nothing. We became experienced with knowing what we could rule out. By the time we made our first wave detection, in 2015, a finding that earned LIGO founders a physics Nobel in 2017, we had published about 100 papers reporting null results.

One such null case was in 2010. We were completing a science run, in which data are collected for a set period of time, and had a candidate for a striking event — it looked like we’d finally got there. But we knew it might be a ‘blind injection’, which is when a false signal is inserted into a data set by authorized colleagues to test our analyses.

We finished the analysis, drafted the paper and then asked the LIGO director to open a sealed envelope to tell us whether this was a real event or not. It wasn’t, but the exercise revealed a real problem: the sky location our analysis recovered didn’t match the signal’s known location. Two of the detector’s mirrors had moved in the wrong direction. We found the glitch in about a day. This showed we could efficiently self-correct when detecting a real sign — which happened five years later.

Recent findings suggest that I tell my students that scientists make lots of mistakes. We’re careful with cross-checks and analyse results carefully, so we catch almost all of them. Some are caught in minutes, some in days and some take more work. This one, because we’d built a test designed to assess itself, took about a day. That’s really the goal: not avoiding mistakes, but rather building enough ways to catch them promptly. Knowing what it means to find nothing is key; it’s a real scientific skill.

Chemist Omar Yaghi (second row, fifth from right), with his team at Tsinghua University in Beijing, indicates that professors can learn notable lessons from their students if they listen to them.Credit: Yaghi Group Photo.

Chemist at Tsinghua University in Beijing and a co-recipient of the 2025 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work with metal–organic frameworks.

In a recent development, back in the 1990s, I was an assistant professor at Arizona State University in Tempe. My team had begun research trying to make inorganic porous materials. These are solid materials with a network of tiny, connected pores that act like molecular sponges to trap molecules, such as wastewater contaminants and toxic gases, on their surfaces. We were successful: we had a paper1 published in the Journal of the American Chemical Society and, later, in Science2.

It has been revealed that then a doctoral student came looking to join my lab. She didn’t sound very confident, her English was not so good and it wasn’t the right time of year to look for a PhD adviser. I made up some reason not to take her. But she kept coming back and was adamant about working with me.

So I accepted her into my lab group, and she started working on metal–organic compounds, another type of porous material. I felt that this was a waste of time: researchers had known about these structures since the 1950s, but nothing useful had resulted from them. Once you emptied their solvent-filled pores to trap other molecules, such as gases, they collapsed and became useless. I used to call them sculptures: they had beauty, but no function.

It has been revealed that she kept at it, and I held onto my scepticism. After a year, we sat down to discuss her results. That was when I realized that there was an opportunity there: we could make robust metal–organic compounds, after all.

Sources indicate that metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are also materials full of tiny pores. But what makes them particularly interesting is that scientists can adjust the size and shape of those pores, as well as the chemical properties inside them. This makes MOFs more tunable than inorganic porous materials such as zeolites and much better at trapping some gases. Some MOFs can drive chemical reactions, some conduct electricity and some are stable enough to be reused.

My student found strong chemical bindings that gave stability to early versions of these structures and, within a very short period, our findings were published in Nature3. It had worked.

Decades later, I met with my former student, and she told me that she had been struggling back then and wanted to try her luck with me, a newly introduced professor at the time, because no one else would take her in.

I think science is the greatest equalizer. One discovery can take you from humble beginnings, as it did for us, and propel you to the top of your profession.

According to recent reports, I had an opinion about an area of research and didn’t listen to my student, and, to that student’s credit, she persisted. To my credit, I changed my thinking. Neither the student nor the professor can afford to do science without the other.

In a recent development, plant geneticist Chris Martine’s misidentified sample led to the identification of a new species of bush tomato plant in northern Australia. Credit: Jason Cantley.

Plant geneticist at Bucknell University in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, and president of the Botanical Society of America.

According to recent reports, I’ve studied Australia’s bush tomatoes for about 25 years. My team was the first to describe Solanum ossicruentum, nicknamed the blood bone tomato because it seems to bleed when cut open. It got us some press coverage and was a major deal for our laboratory in 20164.

It has been revealed that in 2017, Angela McDonnell, a postdoc, joined us. We started a major genetics project to build an evolutionary tree to understand the family history of the bush tomatoes we had been studying for years. We had two samples of S. ossicruentum from two locations: the Tanami Desert and the Keep River National Park, both in northern Australia. When the results of testing came back, genomic differences landed them in totally different places on the evolutionary tree of the group.

According to recent reports, in my mind, there was no way it was possible. I’d identified the specimens myself. I assumed we’d mislabelled something. I asked Angela to check everything carefully, but she was certain that wasn’t the case. To me it didn’t add up — I came close to saying, “let’s just pull the misplaced one and call it an error”.

Two years ago, while looking through the folders of S. ossicruentum specimens at the Northern Territory Herbarium in Palmerston, Australia, I noticed some that had strange dots on the backs of their leaves. At first, I thought it was mildew, but then I wondered whether these dots were extrafloral nectaries, or nectar-producing glands found outside the plant’s flower. Then I realized the plants with such dots were mostly from one part of Australia, the northern edge of the Tanami Desert — exactly where I was heading next.

When I got there, plants with these little dots were dripping with nectar with ants harvesting it, an interaction I hadn’t seen to this level before. I checked whether Angela’s big phylogeny project had anything from that region, and there it was — the misplaced plant. The two samples of what I thought were S. ossicruentum belonged in two different places on the evolutionary tree because they were two different species. Indeed, that initial sample’s evolutionary tree placement was the best evidence for the latest species that we later described: Solanum nectarifolium5. My first thought was to thank Angela for not pulling that specimen out of our analysis. I was honestly thrilled.

Before that, I had felt overconfident in what I knew, and Angela was certain that this was a carefully curated data set and a rigorously achieved genetic result. As I’ve become more senior, I’ve become more comfortable with uncertainty: when something doesn’t fit our preconceived ideas, that’s an interesting result — that’s how you find more fresh things.

Sources indicate that now I realize how key it is for people who are more junior than myself to speak up and share their ideas, especially when they run counter to convention. If we look back at the history of science, that’s the only way we’ve progressed.

Palaeontologist Catherine Badgley says that a key skill for scientists is knowing when to stop pursuing a good idea that simply isn’t working. Credit: David Bay.

Palaeontologist at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor.

Industry observers note that in the 1990s, I was an associate research scientist in the University of Michigan’s Museum of Paleontology. Serge Legendre, a colleague who was then at the University of Montpellier in France, highlighted me a newly introduced way, at the time, of explaining body-size distributions in fossils of extinct mammalian species. He used cenograms — a graphical technique that ranks mammalian species in a community by body size.

In well-watered ecosystems, there was a fairly continuous line: all species were closely spaced in size. But habitats with long dry seasons had a big gap in the middle where medium-sized mammals would be — an interesting mystery. Legendre found that many animals in that size range are fruit-eaters, and fruit isn’t available in arid or very cold environments all year long. If the theory was correct, we might be able to infer past climate from the sizes of mammals in fossil communities.

It has been revealed that I had a lot of climate data for mammal locations worldwide, so the two of us, as well as palaeontologist Philip Gingerich, who was then also at the University of Michigan, decided to build a much larger database of locations and add climate variables. We wanted to determine whether climate variables could predict the size gap we saw. I was excited enough that I wrote it up as a book proposal and received a contract from the University of Chicago Press.

Recent findings suggest that but the more data that we collected, the fuzzier the picture became. After more than a year, I had written four chapters. But I had to admit we had fewer results than when we started.

Industry observers note that I knew the data weren’t flawed because I had used this enormous mammalian fossil database successfully for other research projects. For example, undergraduate students used it to show that the length of the growing season, as a climate variable, could be used to predict the number of fruit- and plant-eating species at a given time.

It has been revealed that I eventually realized that each continent has its own evolutionary history and its own climatic circumstances — no one is exactly like another. Our largest data sets, from Africa and North America, have almost completely non-overlapping climates, so one was never going to be a good model for predicting the other.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, U.S. flights delays eased on Monday as airlines scrambled to get back on track after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded departures nationwide for more than four hours on Friday.

Nearly 300 U.S. flights were canceled and close to 1,000 were delayed Monday, a fraction of Sunday's disruptions, according to FlightAware data.

Industry observers note that transportation Secretary Sean Duffy over the weekend tied the glitch that prompted officials to call for the ground stop to a router in southern Arkansas and work to enhancement copper wires to a fiber-optic system overseen by L3Harris Technologies. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said the upgrades were part of "routine" maintenance to switch over to fiber optic.

According to recent reports, officials ordered the ground stop before 4 p.m. ET on Friday and it lasted until after 8 p.m. ET, marking the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

In a recent development, hundreds of thousands of travelers were stranded and about 18,000 U.S. flights were canceled from Friday through Monday morning, according to FlightAware.

Over that period, American Airlines had the most cancellations with 5,367 flights, close to 22% of its schedule, followed by Delta Air Lines with 3,434 cancellations, or 17% of its schedule, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Southwest Airlines and United Airlines each canceled more than 16% of their schedules. Bad weather on Thursday and Friday had also contributed to disruptions before the ground stop.

On Sunday, disruptions lingered but were starting to improve.

It has been revealed that "We slept here," stated Beth Martin, who was trying to travel home to Birmingham, Alabama, from Newly introduced York's LaGuardia Airport on Sunday at the end of her daughter's birthday trip. The two were booked for Saturday night, and when delay announcements started rolling in from Delta, they decided to make good use of the extra time: After strolling through Central Park, they went window shopping on Fifth Avenue.

But when the flight was canceled, the standby list for a backup flight looked grim and their original midtown hotel was charging about $700 for an additional night, the two slept at LaGuardia on Saturday. She said they found wheelchairs to sleep in outside security.

Airlines waived change fees and fare differences and offered pilots and flight attendants extra pay to ease the delays.

Customers told CNBC they were booked on several flights before getting on board.

It has been revealed that justine Fritz, who works in sales for a consumer goods company, was in Newly introduced York for a business event on Friday. She tried five different flights before getting on one to Houston, then flew four hours out of her way to get back to Minneapolis after her Saturday flight was canceled. Fritz said she had so many boarding passes that the Transportation Security Administration wouldn't let her through security at first.

"It's been bananas," she told CNBC at the gate. Fritz remarked she made the best of it by shopping and getting a haircut, but she's still disappointed.

"I'm missing the first hour of the Vikings game," she said.

Martin said her trip home with her daughter will take even longer. Delta booked them to Memphis, and her husband will drive the four hours from Birmingham to pick them up.

Officials are investigating the root cause that led to what the FAA described as "instability" in data feeds. Duffy said Sunday that two routers, the original one detected as a problem in southern Arkansas, and another in Amarillo, Texas, are in an L3Harris lab in Florida.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," L3Harris said in a statement Saturday afternoon.

President Donald Trump remarked Monday he didn't "take any responsibility" for the ground stop.

Shortly after the ground stop, Duffy stated he was asking Congress for as much as $50 billion for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system. A day later, Democratic lawmakers pushed back, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Recent findings suggest that "Our committee, on behalf of the flying public, will hold the administration accountable for what happened to make sure this chaos does not happen again," said Reps. Rick Larsen, D.-Wash., ranking member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and Andre Carson, D.-Ind., ranking member of the aviation subcommittee, in a joint statement.

Astronomers discover a dead star spinning every 8 minutes and sending mysterious radio pulses

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth.
  • The discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR).
  • The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that astronomers have traced mysterious radio signals to an unusual pair of stars more than 5,000 light-years from Earth. One is a dead star that rotates every eight minutes, while its companion closely resembles our own Sun.

The discovery was made by researchers at the Curtin University branch of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR). Their findings reveal a previously unseen combination of stars producing radio pulses and offer new clues about the origins of some of the Milky Way's most puzzling signals.

The stellar system, designated GPM J071507−114153, contains a white dwarf and a G-type star orbiting one another. A white dwarf is the extremely dense remnant of a star that has exhausted its nuclear fuel and shed its outer layers. Its companion belongs to the same general category of stars as the Sun.

Sources indicate that until now, astronomers had detected similar radio pulses in systems containing white dwarfs and smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs. This marks the first time such signals have been identified in a system where a white dwarf orbits a Sun-like star.

A Rare Star System With Mysterious Radio Pulses.

In a recent development, the newly identified pair belongs to an unusual group of astronomical objects called long-period transients (LPTs). These objects produce radio emissions that appear and disappear over periods lasting anywhere from several minutes to hours.

Despite growing interest in these strange signals, their origins remain poorly understood. The same ICRAR research team discovered the first known example in 2021, and only about a dozen have been identified since then.

Some of these systems contain a white dwarf alongside another star, but astronomers have struggled to determine which member of the pair is responsible for the radio emissions.

The latest discovery provides an notable breakthrough. For the first time, researchers have obtained radio observations detailed enough to follow a white dwarf as it travels around its stellar companion. This allows them to pinpoint the likely location of the radio pulses much more accurately.

It has been revealed that "This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," said lead author Dr. Sam McSweeney.

McSweeney, now a commissioning scientist with the Square Kilometre Array Observatory, made the discovery while working at Curtin University's ICRAR branch.

To confirm the findings and examine the white dwarf's orbital motion, the researchers analyzed more than 100 hours of radio observations using computing resources at the Pawsey Supercomputing Research Centre.

Giant Magnetic Storms Detected 5,000 Light-Years Away.

The radio signals revealed more than the movement of the dead star. They also gave astronomers a surprising opportunity to investigate magnetic activity on its Sun-like companion.

In a recent development, according to study co-author Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, the observations exposed stellar flares associated with powerful magnetic disturbances. Similar magnetic processes on our own Sun can lead to auroras on Earth when energetic particles interact with our planet's magnetic field and atmosphere.

The team also detected evidence that the white dwarf passed behind an especially magnetically active region near its companion.

"As a bonus, we also saw the white dwarf moving behind a region with a strong magnetic field, most likely a 'stellar prominence', which is a large loop of plasma erupting from a star's surface.".

In a recent development, A stellar prominence consists of electrically charged gas held in enormous loops by magnetic fields. These structures can extend far above a star's surface, providing clues about the powerful forces shaping its outer atmosphere.

The ability to detect such activity across thousands of light-years demonstrates how much information astronomers can extract from radio signals, even when the stars themselves are extraordinarily distant.

"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away.".

Powerful Radio Telescopes Reveal a Hidden Stellar Pair.

ICRAR researchers have played a leading role in identifying long-period transients, and the latest discovery relied on observations from several major astronomical facilities around the world.

The system was initially detected during a sweeping radio survey of the Milky Way conducted with the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) in Western Australia.

According to recent reports, "We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," noted Associate Professor Hurley-Walker.

According to recent reports, after the radio telescopes narrowed down the system's location, astronomers turned to the W.M. Keck Observatory on Maunakea, Hawaiʻi Island. Optical observations confirmed that the radio source was associated with a G-type star, establishing the presence of a companion similar to the Sun.

The MWA, led by Curtin University, operates at Inyarrimanha Ilgari Bundara, the CSIRO Murchison Radio-Astronomy Observatory on Wajarri Yamaji Country in Western Australia.

The MeerKAT telescope was built and is operated by the South African Radio Astronomy Observatory in South Africa's North Cape province.

Both instruments are precursors to the next generation of Square Kilometre Array telescopes. The Australian facility, SKA-Low, and the South African facility, SKA-Mid, are being developed to provide much greater sensitivity and detail when observing the radio universe.

For astronomers studying rare stellar systems, these future capabilities could dramatically expand the number of objects they can discover and reveal much more about the processes responsible for their unusual signals.

Dr. McSweeney said, "If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find, and what a beautifully detailed view of their signals we will have, once the SKAO telescopes are completely built.".

The findings were published in Nature Astronomy in a study titled "A long-period transient with a Sun-like companion.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.

The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven.".

As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued... without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected.".

However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.

Sources indicate that "What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.

"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.

However, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights.".

Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.

Sources indicate that "That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.

The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.

Zverev's lawyers reject the allegations.

Recent findings suggest that "Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.

In a recent development, "Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view.".

The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press.".

Scheele remarked he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.

Industry observers note that "We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he mentioned. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.

"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice.".

Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is presently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

#36302. Breaking: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1684 w)

Breaking: MIT discovers that aging weakens the brain’s nighttime cleaning system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste.
  • Industry observers note that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults.
  • Recent findings suggest that the findings raise important questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

While we sleep, the brain carries out an essential maintenance process that helps wash away accumulated waste. But newly introduced research from MIT suggests that this natural cleaning system becomes less effective as we grow older, revealing another way aging can change the brain beyond simply disrupting sleep.

Industry observers note that researchers discovered that waves of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), which help carry waste out of the brain, are significantly weaker in older adults. The decline appears to be connected to changes in the slow electrical waves that occur during deep sleep, as well as changes in how blood moves through the brain. Importantly, the reduced fluid movement cannot be explained simply by older people spending less time asleep.

Recent findings suggest that the findings raise important questions about whether weakened brain cleansing could contribute to Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. The team now hopes to determine whether changes in these fluid waves could eventually help identify people at greater risk of cognitive decline.

Sources indicate that "We know that people age really differently. Some people age very successfully with great cognitive outcomes, and other people develop cognitive decline. If we can figure out who has great trajectories of aging and what are the factors that are associated with that, we might be able to use that to predict future outcomes," notes Laura Lewis, the Athinoula A. Martinos Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, a member of MIT's Institute for Medical Engineering and Science and the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and an associate member of the Picower Institute for Learning and Memory.

Lewis and her colleagues also want to investigate whether treatments or other interventions could strengthen this waste-clearing process in older adults.

The study was published in Nature Aging, with Lewis serving as senior author. Its lead authors are Sydney Bailes, a postdoctoral researcher in MIT's Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems, and Stephanie Williams, a former MIT visiting student who received her PhD from Boston University in 2026.

How Deep Sleep Helps the Brain Clear Waste.

According to recent reports, deep sleep does much more than leave us feeling refreshed. During its deepest stages, known as non-REM sleep, the brain produces powerful, slow electrical waves that support physical recovery, strengthen memories, and help regulate other essential functions.

It has been revealed that in 2019, Lewis and her colleagues discovered that these slow brain waves also help generate rhythmic movements of cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid moves through spaces around the brain and plays an vital role in carrying away waste products.

That earlier discovery led to a latest question. Because slow brain waves typically weaken with age, could the fluid movements responsible for clearing waste also become less effective?

Previous research had produced conflicting results. Some studies suggested that cerebrospinal fluid movement declined with age, while others reported increases. However, those investigations had not directly monitored the fluid during sleep, when the brain's natural cleaning activity is especially important.

To investigate, the MIT team recruited two groups of volunteers. Younger participants were between 18 and 39 years old, while the older group ranged from 60 to 84.

Each volunteer completed a testing session lasting approximately two hours. The sessions began late at night, increasing the likelihood that participants would become sleepy during the measurements.

The researchers combined several techniques to observe what was happening inside the brain. Functional magnetic resonance imaging, or fMRI, allowed them to track changes in cerebral blood flow. A specialized MRI method developed by Lewis measured cerebrospinal fluid movement, while electroencephalography, or EEG, recorded the brain's electrical activity.

Many participants fell asleep inside the scanner, providing an opportunity to compare their brain activity and fluid movements during wakefulness and sleep.

According to recent reports, the results revealed a striking age difference. As younger adults entered non-REM sleep, their slow brain waves grew stronger and were accompanied by larger waves of cerebrospinal fluid. In older adults, however, the average fluid waves were substantially smaller.

The findings showed that aging was associated with a weakening of the fluid movements that normally accompany deep sleep.

Why the Aging Brain's Cleaning Waves Weaken.

Sources indicate that the researchers next investigated what might be causing this decline. In a separate set of experiments conducted while participants were fully awake, they examined how the brain's blood vessels responded to different demands.

One possible explanation involved neurovascular coupling, the process that connects brain activity with blood flow.

When a particular region of the brain becomes more active, its cells require additional oxygen and nutrients. Nearby blood vessels normally widen to deliver more blood, ensuring that the active cells receive the resources they need.

In a recent development, to measure this response, the researchers showed volunteers a flickering checkerboard pattern while monitoring blood flow with fMRI. The rapidly changing visual pattern stimulates activity in regions involved in processing vision, which should trigger an increase in local blood supply.

In many older participants, the brain's electrical activity increased as expected, but the corresponding rise in blood flow was much smaller. This suggested that aging had weakened the ability of blood vessels to respond to the brain's changing oxygen requirements.

The team then performed a second experiment to examine the brain's broader vascular responsiveness.

Sources indicate that participants were instructed to hold their breath while researchers monitored changes in cerebral blood flow. Holding one's breath causes carbon dioxide to accumulate in the bloodstream, which normally prompts blood vessels in the brain to widen and increase blood flow.

Sources indicate that once again, the older group showed a weaker response. On average, their cerebral blood flow increased less than it did in younger volunteers.

Together, these experiments indicated that changes in the brain's vascular system could help explain why its waste-clearing fluid waves diminish with age.

Sources indicate that using a statistical model, the scientists found that weakened neurovascular coupling and reduced blood flow responses accounted for much of the decline in cerebrospinal fluid movement. However, the two mechanisms did not explain the entire difference, suggesting that additional biological changes associated with aging are also involved.

"Aging is so complex, and so many different things change, that it's really hard to disentangle the individual factors," Bailes indicates. "We try to account for some of the mechanisms, but there definitely are a lot of other factors related to vascular health and lifestyle. If you were able to measure all of them, you might be able to break it apart into different explanations for why an individual's CSF flow might be more or less impaired.".

Could Weaker Brain Cleansing Increase Dementia Risk?

The discovery may have vital implications for understanding neurological diseases associated with aging.

According to recent reports, earlier studies have linked disrupted sleep to a greater risk of Alzheimer's disease and other forms of dementia. Because cerebrospinal fluid helps remove waste from the brain, researchers are particularly interested in whether age-related changes in its movement might contribute to neurodegeneration.

Industry observers note that none of the volunteers in the MIT study had been diagnosed with a neurodegenerative disorder. However, brain scans revealed that some older participants showed signs of gray matter atrophy, meaning a loss of brain tissue in regions containing large numbers of nerve cells.

Those changes were associated with greater reductions in cerebrospinal fluid movement.

Sources indicate that the relationship does not establish that weakened fluid flow causes brain tissue loss or dementia. Nevertheless, it provides a reason to investigate whether these changes might serve as early warning signs of neurological decline.

The researchers hope to follow some of the participants over time to determine whether reduced cerebrospinal fluid movement is associated with a greater likelihood of developing a neurodegenerative condition.

Can the Brain's Nighttime Cleaning System Be Restored?

Beyond understanding why brain cleansing declines, the MIT team is exploring whether it might be possible to improve the process.

One promising possibility involves sound stimulation during sleep.

It has been revealed that in a separate recent study, Lewis' laboratory found that brief bursts of "pink noise" could increase cerebrospinal fluid movement in younger adults. Pink noise is a type of sound that contains a broad range of frequencies, with greater emphasis on lower frequencies than white noise.

Although the approach has shown potential in younger people, researchers have not yet tested whether it can produce similar effects in older adults.

Another intriguing finding could provide clues about how to preserve the brain's natural cleaning abilities.

Recent findings suggest that while older participants generally had weaker cerebrospinal fluid waves than younger adults, the decline was not universal. Some older volunteers retained fluid movements that were comparable to those measured in healthy younger people.

This raises the possibility that certain biological or lifestyle factors may help protect the brain's waste-removal system against aging.

Industry observers note that "It's really intriguing that for some of these older adults, their CSF fell right in the range of the healthy young adults," Lewis notes. "We are really interested in what's different in those people and how that might be related to future health outcomes.".

Understanding why some older brains maintain these youthful fluid movements could ultimately help researchers identify ways to support healthier brain aging and investigate whether preserving the brain's nighttime cleaning system can reduce the risk of cognitive decline.

The research received funding from the National Institutes of Health, the Simons Collaboration on Plasticity in the Aging Brain, a McKnight Scholar Award, a Pew Biomedical Scholar Award, an MIT EECS Transformative Research Award, the Picower Institute Neurological Disorder Discovery Research Fund, a Sloan Fellowship, and the Department of Defense National Defense Science and Engineering Graduate Fellowship Program.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • When NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary.
  • Now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds.
  • The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When NASA's Voyager 2 spacecraft visited Uranus and Neptune in the 1980s, it discovered something extraordinary. Unlike Earth, which has a relatively orderly magnetic field with clearly defined north and south poles, both distant planets possess strangely distorted and dramatically tilted magnetic fields. For decades, scientists have struggled to explain why.

Now, researchers believe they may have found an answer hidden deep inside these enormous worlds. A upcoming study suggests that changes in how well materials conduct electricity under extreme conditions could explain the planets' unusual magnetism. The findings also raise an intriguing possibility: the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may change dramatically over just a few decades.

The research, published in Communications Physics, was led by scientists at The University of Texas at Austin in collaboration with researchers from the University of California, Los Angeles, Imperial College London, and Northumbria University.

Why Uranus and Neptune Have Such Strange Magnetic Fields.

According to recent reports, planetary magnetic fields originate deep beneath the surface, where moving fluids capable of conducting electricity generate magnetic forces. Scientists call this process a dynamo.

Recent findings suggest that on Earth, the dynamo operates within the outer core, a layer of molten metal surrounded by mostly solid rock. As liquid iron circulates and the planet rotates, it generates a magnetic field resembling that of a giant bar magnet. This produces the familiar north and south magnetic poles that allow compasses to point in a consistent direction.

Earth's magnetic field is also closely aligned with its rotation axis. Its main magnetic axis, known as a dipole, is tilted by only 11 degrees. Uranus and Neptune are strikingly different. Uranus has a magnetic dipole tilted by 59 degrees, while Neptune's is tilted by 47 degrees.

Explaining these extreme tilts requires a better understanding of what lies inside the two planets.

Uranus and Neptune are classified as ice giants, a name that reflects their presumed composition rather than suggesting they are simply frozen worlds. Each is approximately four times wider than Earth, and scientists believe their interiors contain substantial amounts of hydrogen, helium, water, ammonia, methane, and rocky material. However, their precise internal compositions remain uncertain.

Extreme Conditions Deep Inside the Ice Giants.

Chi Yan, the study's lead author and a research associate at the UT Jackson School of Geosciences, believes the combination of the planets' enormous size and unusual chemical makeup may help explain their distorted magnetic fields.

Sources indicate that "Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," stated Yan. "Under these conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth.".

Ions are electrically charged particles that can carry electric current. If the materials inside Uranus and Neptune become more conductive at greater depths, that could significantly influence how their magnetic fields are generated.

To investigate this possibility, the researchers developed computer simulations designed to reproduce the strange magnetic fields recorded by Voyager 2.

Their models assumed that electrical conductivity increases deeper inside the planets. The researchers also tested a variety of possible internal structures, examining how circulating fluids, temperature changes, and magnetic forces interact over time.

The results suggest that these changing electrical properties could play a crucial role in producing the unusual magnetic fields observed around both ice giants.

Magnetic Poles Could Shift Dramatically Within Decades.

Perhaps the most surprising finding is that the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may be far less stable than Earth's.

According to recent reports, according to the simulations, their magnetic axes could undergo substantial changes in relatively short periods. In some scenarios, the magnetic tilt shifted by tens of degrees within only a few decades.

That raises the possibility that the magnetic fields surrounding Uranus and Neptune today are significantly different from those measured when Voyager 2 flew past them in the 1980s.

"Earth's magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," remarked Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others it shifts only slightly over the same span.".

Recent findings suggest that these dramatic changes remain predictions from computer models rather than confirmed observations. However, scientists may already have a way to look for evidence of them.

James Webb Telescope Could Reveal Magnetic Changes.

It has been revealed that researchers are now examining detailed infrared images of Uranus and Neptune captured by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). They are particularly interested in the planets' auroras, which form when charged particles from the Sun interact with gases in their atmospheres.

Auroras are closely connected to planetary magnetic fields, making them valuable clues to what is happening far above the planets' hidden interiors. Changes in the appearance and arrangement of these glowing atmospheric features could help researchers determine whether the magnetic poles have shifted since Voyager 2's encounters.

"We are busy working on what's contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere, promises to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, an notable stepping stone," mentioned Tom Stallard, a professor at Northumbria University who led the JWST observation campaign and reviewed the paper for the journal.

The ionosphere is a region of the upper atmosphere containing electrically charged particles. Its behavior is influenced by magnetic activity, offering another potential source of information about the planets' changing magnetic environments.

It has been revealed that the research team hopes to combine Webb's auroral observations with Voyager 2's original magnetic field measurements and the latest dynamo simulations. Together, these sources of evidence could provide the clearest picture yet of how the magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune are arranged today.

Even so, scientists emphasize that fully understanding the planets' deep interiors will require upcoming spacecraft missions to these distant worlds. Until then, improved simulations and powerful telescopes may help unravel one of the solar system's most unusual magnetic mysteries.

The research was funded by The University of Texas Institute for Geophysics (UTIG) in the Jackson School of Geosciences, the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA), and the Science and Technology Facilities Council.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role.
  • "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Robert Pattinson has been cast as the next James Bond in the upcoming film from director Denis Villeneuve. It will be the 26th James Bond film and the first since Amazon MGM took over the iconic franchise.

Recent findings suggest that pattinson will be the seventh actor to play the role. Monday's announcement — which came in part via an Instagram post — ends a long period of speculation about who would take over as "007" after Daniel Craig.

"James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime," Pattinson said in a statement. "I couldn't be more excited about this partnership and the work ahead with this fantastic team.".

Pattinson has appeared in several big-ticket films this year, including Christopher Nolan's "The Odyssey" and psychological thriller "Primetime," and he'll soon appear in "Dune: Part Three," also directed by Villeneuve. Pattinson, who rose to fame with the Twilight movie series, is also in production for Matt Reeves' "The Batman Part II," a follow-up to the 2022 film based on the DC comic.

The upcoming Bond film will have a script by Steven Knight and will be produced by Amy Pascal, known for her work on the Spider-Man franchise, and David Heyman, who produced all eight Harry Potter films.

Recent findings suggest that "We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve mentioned. "I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our fresh James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin.".

In 2022, Amazon bought MGM Studios, which had long produced the Bond movies, for roughly $8.45 billion. Amazon MGM then acquired creative control of the James Bond intellectual property rights in 2025, when it closed a deal with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson.

The film is still untitled, and Amazon MGM hasn't announced a projected release date.

#36295. Breaking: A latest approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine highlights early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1457 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 CNN ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: A latest approach to a Covid-19 nasal vaccine highlights early promise

📅 03 Apr 2023 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1457 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNN

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.
  • In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.
  • WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists in Germany say they’ve been able to make a nasal vaccine that can shut down a Covid-19 infection in the nose and throat, where the virus gets its first foothold in the body.

In experiments in hamsters, two doses of the vaccine – which is made with a live but weakened form of the coronavirus that causes Covid-19 – blocked the virus from copying itself in the animals’ upper airways, achieving “sterilizing immunity” and preventing illness, a long-sought goal of the pandemic.

WHO experts revise Covid-19 vaccine advice, say healthy kids and teens low risk.

Although this vaccine has several more hurdles to clear before it gets to a doctor’s office or drug store, other nasal vaccines are in use or are nearing the finish line in clinical trials.

Industry observers note that china and India both rolled out vaccines given through the nasal tissues last fall, though it’s not clear how well they may be working. Studies on the effectiveness of these vaccines have yet to be published, leaving much of the world to wonder whether this approach to protection really works in people.

The US has reached something of a stalemate with Covid-19. Even with the darkest days of the pandemic behind us, hundreds of Americans are still dying daily as the infection continues to simmer in the background of our return to normal life.

As long as the virus continues to spread among people and animals, there’s always the potential for it mutate into a more contagious or more damaging version of itself. And while Covid infections have become manageable for most healthy people, they may still pose a danger to vulnerable groups such as the elderly and immunocompromised.

Researchers hope next-generation Covid-19 vaccines, which aim to shut down the virus before it ever gets a chance to make us sick and ultimately prevent the spread of infection, could make our newest resident respiratory infection less of a threat.

China approves its first mRNA Covid-19 vaccine.

One way scientists are trying to do that is by boosting mucosal immunity, beefing up immune defenses in the tissues that line the upper airways, right where the virus would land and begin to infect our cells.

It’s a bit like stationing firefighters underneath the smoke alarm in your house, states study author Emanuel Wyler, a scientist at the Max Delbruck Center for Molecular Medicine in the Helmholtz Association in Berlin.

The immunity that’s created by shots works throughout the body, but it resides primarily in the blood. That means it may take longer to mount a response.

“If they are already on site, they can immediately eliminate the fire, but if they’re like 2 miles away, they first need to drive there, and by that time, one-third of the house is already in full flames,” Wyler noted.

Recent findings suggest that mucosal vaccines are also better at priming a different kind of first responder than injections do. They do a better job of summoning IgA antibodies, which have four arms to grab onto invaders instead of the two arms that the y-shaped IgG antibodies have. Some scientists think IgA antibodies may be less picky about their targets than IgG antibodies, which makes them better equipped to deal with new variants.

The fresh nasal vaccine takes a new approach to a very old idea: weakening a virus so it’s no longer a threat and then giving it to people so their immune systems can learn to recognize and fight it off. The first vaccines using this approach date to the 1870s, against anthrax and rabies. Back then, scientists weakened the agents they were using with heat and chemicals.

According to recent reports, the researchers manipulated the genetic material in the virus to make it harder for cells to translate. This technique, called codon pair deoptimization, hobbles the virus so it can be shown to the immune system without making the body sick.

According to recent reports, “You could imagine reading a text … and every letter is a different font, or every letter is a different size, then the text is much harder to read. And this is basically what we do in codon pair deoptimization,” Wyler remarked.

In the hamster studies, which were published Monday in the journal Nature Microbiology, two doses of the live but weakened nasal vaccine created a much stronger immune response than either two doses of an mRNA-based vaccine or one that uses an adenovirus to ferry the vaccine instructions into cells.

The researchers think the live weakened vaccine probably worked better because it closely mimics the process of a natural infection.

The nasal vaccine also previews the entire coronavirus for the body, not just its spike proteins like current Covid-19 vaccines do, so the hamsters were able to make immune weapons against a wider range of targets.

It has been revealed that as promising as all this sounds, vaccine experts say caution is warranted. This vaccine still has to pass more tests before it’s ready for use, but they say the results look encouraging.

Health officials consider another round of bivalent boosters for the most vulnerable Americans.

“They did a very nice job. This is obviously a competent and thoughtful team that did this work, and impressive in the scope of what they did. Now it just needs to be repeated,” perhaps in primates and certainly in humans before it can be widely used, said Dr. Greg Poland, who designs vaccines at the Mayo Clinic. He was not involved in the fresh research.

The study began in 2021, before the Omicron variant was around, so the vaccine tested in these experiments was made with the original strain of the coronavirus. In the experiments, when they infected animals with Omicron, the live but weakened nasal vaccine still performed better than the others, but its ability to neutralize the virus was diminished. Researchers think it will need an update.

In a recent development, it also needs to be tested in humans, and Wyler states they’re working on that. The scientists have partnered with a Swiss firm called RocketVax to start phase I clinical trials.

Other vaccines are further along, but the progress has been “slow and halting,” Poland said. Groups working on these vaccines are struggling to raise the steep costs of getting a latest vaccine to market, and they’re doing it in a setting where people tend to think the vaccine race has been won and done.

In reality, Poland said, we’re far from that. All it would take is another Omicron-level shift in the evolution of the virus, and we could be back at square one, with no effective tools against the coronavirus.

“That’s foolish. We should be developing a pan-coronavirus vaccine that does induce mucosal immunity and that is long-lived,” he noted.

At least four nasal vaccines for Covid-19 have reached late-stage testing in people, according to the World Health Organization’s vaccine tracker.

The nasal vaccines in use in China and India rely on harmless adenoviruses to ferry their instructions into cells, although effectiveness data for these has not been published.

Two other nasal vaccines are finishing human studies.

Covid vaccine maker Novavax indicates it may not survive.

One, a recombinant vaccine that can be produced cheaply in chicken eggs, the same way many flu vaccines are, is being put through its paces by researchers at Mount Sinai in Upcoming York City.

Another, like the German vaccine, uses a live but weakened version of the virus. It’s being developed by a company called Codagenix. Results of those studies, which were carried out in South America and Africa, may come later this year.

The German team indicates it’s eagerly watching for the Codagenix data.

“They will be very key in order to know where whether this kind of attempt is basically promising or not,” Wyler said.

It has been revealed that they have reason to worry. Respiratory infections have proved to be tough targets for inhaled vaccines.

FluMist, a live but weakened form of the flu virus, works reasonably well in children but doesn’t help adults as much. The reason is thought to be that adults already have immune memory for the flu, and when the virus is injected into the nose, the vaccine mostly boosts what’s already there.

Still, some of the most potent vaccines such as the vaccine against measles, mumps and rubella use live attenuated viruses, so it’s a promising approach.

Another consideration is that live vaccines can’t be taken by everyone. People with very compromised immunity are often cautioned against using live vaccines because even these very weakened viruses may be risky for them.

“Although it’s strongly attenuated, it’s still a real virus,” Wyler said, so it would have to be used carefully.

Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.
