⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.
  • Sources indicate that the Pan American Health Organization unveiled the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence.
  • In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking newly introduced ones.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. on Tuesday lost its official designation as a measles-free nation, more than 25 years after it eliminated the highly contagious virus.

Sources indicate that the Pan American Health Organization unveiled the decision, which came after an independent panel of eight scientific experts convened last week to consider the country's epidemiological evidence. The director of PAHO, the regional branch of the World Health Organization, made the final call that measles is endemic — or always present — in the U.S. following 12 months of continuous transmission.

In other words, measles is spreading regularly in the country again, with ongoing outbreaks sparking newly introduced ones.

"The commission concluded that endemic measles transmission has now been reestablished in Bolivia, Mexico and the United States, and recommended that their measles elimination status be withdrawn — a recommendation which I have accepted," Dr. Jarbas Barbosa, PAHO director, said during a news briefing on Tuesday.

It's a devastating step backward for American public health, as declining childhood vaccination rates and vaccine hesitancy fuel outbreaks across the country that have sickened thousands of people and led to a tragic string of preventable deaths. Among the deaths where vaccination status was reported, all were unvaccinated.

In a recent development, more than 5,400 measles cases had been reported nationwide in 2026 as of mid-November, marking the country's worst outbreak in more than three decades. States have confirmed 10 deaths associated with the disease so far in 2026: seven in Pennsylvania, one in Latest York and two in Wisconsin.

According to recent reports, the commission found that out of 52 U.S. states and territories it tracked, 48 experienced measles outbreaks during the reporting period between January 2025 and January 2026, PAHO Assistant Director Dr. Rhonda Sealey-Thomas mentioned during the briefing. But Barbosa said the countries are already taking action to control outbreaks, such as strengthening vaccination, surveillance for timely case detection and outbreak response efforts.

The U.S. in particular has ramped up vaccination efforts to close immunity gaps, particularly in areas with low immunization coverage experiencing outbreaks, said Dr. Daniel Salas, executive manager of PAHO's Special Program for Comprehensive Immunization. He said PAHO expects the U.S. to present its corrective action initiative in the coming weeks, outlining strategies to regain its designation.

In a Tuesday release, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention remarked it will continue to ensure all communities have the resources to prevent and respond to outbreaks and is committed to working with states and other local partners to restore the U.S.'s measles elimination status.

Industry observers note that CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz noted in the release that the measles elimination designation "is not what protects Americans. Vaccination does." She said the agency has invested $100 million in state and local health departments to reach communities where transmission is occurring.

Sources indicate that last week, Schwartz told Reuters that the agency is going to be "doing the same exact thing that we've been doing today" if the U.S. loses its measles-free status.

Industry observers note that the decision also poses a upcoming test for the Trump administration and its Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has taken steps to change recommendations for the childhood measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine and has a long history of questioning its safety without evidence.

But Kennedy, in a Tuesday X post, remarked he continues to recommend MMR vaccination as "the most effective way to prevent measles.".

"We are working to close vaccination gaps and rebuild public trust," Kennedy said. "We will answer families' questions honestly about vaccine benefits and risks and work with trusted health care providers and community leaders to prevent measles, limit its spread, and support timely treatment.".

CNBC previously reported on how the return of measles in the U.S. exposes weaknesses in the nation's public health system that raise concerns about the return of other eliminated diseases. The resurgence of measles exposes eroding trust in health institutions and growing challenges in persuading people to protect themselves, their children and their communities.

Public health experts previously told CNBC that the return of measles ultimately boils down to fewer children getting vaccinated.

The MMR vaccine is about 97% effective against measles after two doses, while a single dose is 93% effective, according to the CDC. Yet data aggregated by the CDC highlights that vaccination coverage for that shot among U.S. kindergarteners fell to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, which is below the 95% threshold public health officials generally recommend to prevent sustained transmission.

The American Medical Association urged the public to get vaccinated after PAHO's announcement.

"We must treat the current measles outbreaks as an urgent call to rebuild trust in science-based recommendations and restore strong, fully-funded public health infrastructure to protect families and communities and prevent the return of diseases once eliminated," AMA President Dr. Willie Underwood noted in a statement.

In a separate statement, the pharmaceutical industry's largest lobbying group called on policymakers to provide "clear, accurate information about the seriousness of measles infection and the effectiveness of vaccines against it, restore and sustain high vaccination coverage in every community, strengthen vaccination efforts, and invest in disease surveillance and rapid outbreak response.".

"We have the tools to eliminate measles again and what we need now is the commitment to use them," stated Dr. Michael Ybarra, chief medical officer of the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America.

Measles isn't just a public health threat — it's also a huge financial burden on the healthcare system, CNBC reported.

Recent findings suggest that based on this year's case count, a new tool developed by researchers at Johns Hopkins University estimates an economic cost of nearly $83 million for the outbreaks. That total includes $56 million in public health response costs, almost $25 million in lost productivity and more than $1.8 million in direct medical expenses.

The U.S. now joins Canada, Spain and the U.K., which all recently lost their measles-free status after a review by experts at the World Health Organization. While the U.S. dropped out of the WHO, it remains a member of PAHO, its Americas branch.

NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange newly introduced world

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (811 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising latest perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.
  • On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system.
  • The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising latest perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos.

In a recent development, "The first thing we stated was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera demonstrated us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole latest world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges.".

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

Industry observers note that when DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an key part of Hera's investigation.

Recent findings suggest that ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify.".

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit.

Recent findings suggest that although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's fresh image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact.

It has been revealed that after a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

In a recent development, "Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!".

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

According to recent reports, byrne was also extremely fast on her feet, as she demonstrated in 1997 during the Cannes Film Festival. During a post-screening party for Warner Bros./Newly introduced Regency’s buzzy period drama “L.A. Confidential” at a vineyard, a tipsy guest fell into the pool. As Variety reported, when Byrne saw what had happened, she “threw off her jacket and shoes and dove into the water for a dramatic rescue, after which she calmly took her seat for the sit-down dinner at fireworks show.”.

Recent findings suggest that born in 1945, Byrne grew up in the shadow of Yankee Stadium in the Bronx. She met her future husband Gerry Byrne — who served as publisher of Variety from 1989 to 2000 and at present is vice chair of Variety parent firm PMC — while he was attending Fordham College in the borough. The two were neighbors, but in a wonderfully Bronx love story touch, Liz Daly met Gerry Byrne one evening during a ride on the D train.

In a recent development, early on, Liz Daly was drawn to New York’s fashion world. She signed with top modeling agencies Mannequin and Ellen Harth and launched her career as the primary designer’s model for top New York retailers Saks Fifth Avenue and Bonwit Teller. In addition to appearing in TV commercials, Byrne spent years as a runway model with Anne Klein, Donna Karan, Oscar de la Renta and Bill Tice. She then spent another decade working with renowned designers Bob Mackie and Ray Aghayan.

It has been revealed that daly and Byrne married in 1969 at the chapel at St. Patrick’s Cathedral, after Gerry Byrne completed a three-year tour with the U.S. Marine Corps in Vietnam. In tribute to her husband’s service, Liz Byrne successfully released a POW bracelet program to honor the sacrifices made by some families. The effort took root after being publicized nationally through coverage in the Newly introduced York Times.

Byrne was a dedicated marathon runner who participated in multiple New York City Marathons as well as runs hosted by the Marines in Washington, D.C. She was active in numerous nonprofits and in entertainment and media industry charitable efforts.

#36211. Newly introduced discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (977 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Newly introduced discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency.
  • Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an crucial clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature.
  • According to recent reports, to understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an crucial clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising upcoming direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

According to recent reports, to understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold.

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

Recent findings suggest that the challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

According to recent reports, superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal.".

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature.

It has been revealed that the new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," notes Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether.".

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together.

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

It has been revealed that an analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

According to recent reports, in conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck.".

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures.".

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

Newly introduced Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue.

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Actors have become increasingly vocal in recent months about their struggles amid the slowdown in production of film and television demonstrates, drawing attention to performers’ hardships in qualifying for their union health plan and even paying their dues.

In a recent development, facing pressure and online criticism to do something more for floundering members, on Friday the actors’ union SAG-AFTRA announced that its national board had voted unanimously to create a public policy-focused task force to advocate for universal healthcare. The group’s new President’s Healthcare Task Force will “mobilize SAG-AFTRA’s collective strength, public influence, and institutional capacity to advance universal access to affordable, comprehensive, and reliable health care,” the union stated.

According to union president Sean Astin, the SAG-AFTRA Health Plan is on strong financial footing but “a subsantial majority of our members do not qualify” by either not earning the requisite minimum of $28,090 or working 108 applicable days per year.

In a recent development, “This Taskforce seeks a new level of participation in the national movement to expand care for everyone,” Astin added. “We will actively engage with policymakers, gather allies and provide a structured way for our members to participate formally in the process. The President’s Healthcare Taskforce will be an instrument of support in the movement for universal healthcare. The President’s Healthcare Taskforce will be an instrument of support in the movement for universal healthcare.”.

It’s a step, though far from a quick-fix solution to the problems that members have grown louder about in recent weeks. In late October, American Horror Story and Glee actor Cheyenne Jackson debuted the “One Job Away” campaign to draw attention to actors in need of one or a few more jobs to qualify for health insurance. “This is systematic. This is like across the whole swath of SAG actors working right now,” he told The Hollywood Reporter at the time.

According to the latest terms the union negotiated with studios and streamers earlier this year, aimed at addressing healthcare inflation, eligibility premiums and the earnings threshold for health insurance will rise slightly in 2027, with more increases coming in the years after.

Some members have also recently faulted the labor group for dropping its COVID-era policy of keeping performers who were behind on their dues in the union. As of Nov. 1, SAG-AFTRA returned to terminating the memberships of actors who owed dues and, according to Variety, thousands have been dropped from the labor group as a result.

Industry observers note that as these concerns were developing, its national board extended union staff leader Duncan Crabtree-Ireland’s contract until 2032 on Oct. 24 and reportedly gave him a 15 percent raise, drawing some further scrutiny. Prior to the reported raise, Crabtree-Ireland, whose title has been expanded to deem him the chief executive officer of the union, was already the highest-paid labor leader in Hollywood with a published gross salary of $1,068,535. The union explained at the time, “The extended term provides for added stability and continuity for the union during a time of unprecedented industry disruption.” But some members found the timing insensitive.

Once seen as a progressive pipe dream, universal healthcare may be becoming more politically palatable after a midterm election that hinged on affordability concerns and amid rampant healthcare inflation. But achieving it would, to say the least, be politically complex and require immense support from many quarters. Still, at a time of major healthcare challenges across the country, the union can at least point to its advocacy as a form of action.

Sources indicate that “The Cat in the Hat” followed in fourth place with $1.6 million from 3,26 locations. Rival estimates expect Warner Bros.’ animated film to add $7 million by Sunday, bringing the animated film’s cumulative gross to $47.26 million.

Bill Hader voices the titular character in the cartoon, which follows the shenanigans that occur after a mischievous, hat-wearing cat arrives to cheer up two siblings who move to a fresh town.

Finally, in fifth place was Columbia Pictures’ “Ghost Soldier.” The William Eubank-directed film earned $700,000 on Friday, coming in just ahead of GKids’ “Godzilla Minus Zero,” which brought in $680,000 on Friday. That puts the “Godzilla Minus One” follow-up at more than $51 million domestically.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Aviation Administration said Tuesday it would pause the installation of new routers after problems with the technology led the agency to glitch a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday.

Industry observers note that tens of thousands of flights were affected by the ground stop, which halted departing flights for more than four hours. It was the longest halt to U.S. flight departures since 9/11.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday that an overloaded router installed in southern Arkansas as part of an upgrade to a system overseen by L3Harris Technologies appeared to overwhelm systems that feed radar and other data for air traffic control.

The Wall Street Journal first reported the news about the pause.

The FAA and Department of Transportation have said L3Harris was working to convert the communications network from copper wires to fiber optic.

Democratic members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science and Transportation this week asked the FAA and the Department of Transportation for clarity on what went wrong.

"Identifying the device that failed does not establish why it failed," the senators wrote in a statement. "Modernization cannot come at the expense of operational safety.".

The agencies have said they are working to figure out the root cause of the problem and have reiterated that there is no indication of a cyberattack or outside threat.

Recent findings suggest that the senators also asked for a briefing with the FAA, L3Harris and Juniper Networks, which is making the new devices, by Monday. They asked the companies to lay out why the operational systems lacked sufficient redundancy and answer other questions about what led to the outage.

CNBC has reached out to L3Harris and Juniper Networks for comment.

Recent findings suggest that duffy on Friday called for Congress to approve $50 billion in funding for upgrades to the aging U.S. air traffic control system, more than he has previously asked for. Democratic lawmakers pushed back on the request, citing unspent money from existing funding, which includes Congress' approval last year of $12.5 billion for airport and air traffic control improvements over five years.

Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz, R-Texas, stated Tuesday that he thinks there will be support for air traffic control modernization, but that the allocation should be specifically for safety upgrades.

Sources indicate that "I don't think the full $50 billion will be funded," he mentioned. "Some of that is not safety related, but we just discussed there, and what I expressed is that the request needs to be focused on safety modernization.".

According to recent reports, duffy dismissed the idea that the router matter had to do with the introduction of artificial intelligence tools and remarked it was "completely unfounded" because the AI system is not in communication with the defective router. He added that the FBI is helping to investigate the root cause of the issue.

Aging equipment and a shortage of air traffic controllers have for years angered airline executives, who have complained about the cost of resulting disruptions.

— CNBC's Phil LeBeau, Leslie Josephs and Justin Papp contributed to this report.

Breaking: Turkey takes control of opposition broadcaster Sozcu TV

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (780 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Another key opposition media outlet in Turkey has been placed under state control.
  • A trustee has also been appointed: The state deposit protection fund, TMSF, which usually administers the assets of insolvent companies, has been put in charge.
  • A large police contingent raided the broadcaster's headquarters in Istanbul, with counterterrorism officers searching the offices.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Another key opposition media outlet in Turkey has been placed under state control. On Tuesday morning, authorities raided the offices of the television broadcaster Sozcu TV and the news portal Sozcu.com.tr, and arrested several executives.

A trustee has also been appointed: The state deposit protection fund, TMSF, which usually administers the assets of insolvent companies, has been put in charge. Sozcu was one of the last substantial media companies in Turkey to regularly report critically on the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.

A large police contingent raided the broadcaster's headquarters in Istanbul, with counterterrorism officers searching the offices. According to Sozcu, its chairwoman, Funda Tuncer Sidali, and Asim Akgul, the former chief executive of the Sozcu group, were among those arrested.

Industry observers note that the broadcaster did not initially announce the appointment of the trustee on its digital channels. It did call on its audience to follow it under a upcoming account. The leader of the main opposition party, Ozgur Ozel, declared on X: "You will never be able to prevent this nation's voice from rising, its rebellion from being heard, its cry from echoing.".

In a recent development, the Istanbul public prosecutor's office has confirmed the arrangements. It justified the investigation with claims of a suspected connection between the owner of Sozcu, Burak Akhay, and the Gülen movement. The Turkish government blames this movement, which was once allied to Erdogan, for the attempted coup in 2016, and has designated it a terrorist organization.

Sources indicate that according to the investigators, Akbay is said to have used foreign bank accounts to finance two companies involved in media activities on behalf of the Gülen movement. They claim there is strong suspicion that he was able, in this way, to hold a leadership position in the organization.

It is not upcoming for the Turkish state to take over media organizations by appointing trustees. Many media companies accused of being close to the Gülen movement were brought under state control in this way after the attempted coup in 2016. What is new is that for about a year now this is also happening to media seen as pro-opposition.

Recent findings suggest that sozcu is not the first opposition broadcaster to be targeted by the authorities. The TELEI TV channel was searched on October 24, 2025. Its editor-in-chief, Merdan Yanardag, was arrested on charges of espionage and remains in custody. The offices of Halk TV were raided on October 14 this year. There, too, a trustee was put in charge.

According to recent reports, in the space of just over a year, three of the most notable opposition television channels have been brought under state control. Observers see this as another step toward an increasingly authoritarian and politically isolated system.

Berk Esen, a political scientist with Sabanci University in Istanbul, sees these measures as a significant weakening of the opposition in the public domain.

Esen told DW that the government may first have acted behind the scenes and tried to bring Sozcu to heel politically. When this didn't succeed, it invoked the judiciary. Esen says Turkey is increasingly moving toward an authoritarian system. The attempt to prevent opposition organizations and media from gaining strength and influence is part of this.

Esen describes the opposition's success in local government elections in March 2024 as a political turning point. Since then, he says, the government has seen its chances of winning political competitions at the ballot box receding. "It's become harder for the AKP to win elections," says Esen. "That's why it's attacking the opposition and the free media both at once.".

Recent findings suggest that several opposition mayors have also been arrested in recent months and replaced by trustees. They include the mayor of Istanbul and presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu, who has been in detention since his arrest in March last year. He is regarded as one of Erdogan's most promising challengers.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Recent findings suggest that the Turkish Journalists' Association (TGC) spoke of a "black winter for press freedom," and announced its solidarity with all those affected. It described the recent developments as a serious attack on press freedom. The fact that a trustee had been appointed, first at Halk TV and now at Sozcu, showed how the media climate in Turkey has deteriorated, it said.

Industry observers note that "These days, too, shall pass," the TGC declared. "When that day comes, those journalists who seek the truth today will be remembered, as will the decisions that prevent the public from hearing that truth.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Parents have their pick of tech gifts for the holiday shopping season, but a fresh report suggests AI toys shouldn't be among them.

In a recent development, the Public Interest Research Group (PIRG), a consumer advocacy nonprofit, recently released the results of its annual toy research. While some AI products made key safety gains compared to last year, others still have inappropriate conversations and pose considerable privacy risks.

The Alilo Smart AI Bunny, for example, told a tester where to search in their house for bleach, defined the word "fetish," discussed specific sexual scenarios, explained why lubricant can be helpful, and suggested using "padded cuffs, soft floggers, or feather ticklers.".

R.J. Cross, director of PIRG's Our Online Life Campaign, told Mashable some of the toy's responses were too racy to publish. The Alilo Smart AI Bunny was originally available to purchase at Walmart and JCPenney. The toy was previously listed on Amazon but was removed after this story's publication. Walmart also removed a third-party listing for the toy after PIRG reached out to the retailer about the product.

"The market's clearly in its early stages and these are products that are not ready for primetime," Cross remarked, adding that the toys are often glitchy and feel rushed.

Given the research findings, Cross mentioned she personally wouldn't purchase an AI toy for any of the children in her life at this time.

PIRG researchers retested four AI toys (Alilo's Smart AI Bunny, Curio's Grok, FoloToy's Kumma, Miko's Miko 3) and three latest AI toys (Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti, GoLabs AI's Panda, and Ropet's Kamomo).

In testing last year, the Alilo bunny's guardrails also deteriorated during longer exchanges. Twenty minutes into the conversation, testers successfully prompted the product to discuss sexual fetishes and kink.

Recent findings suggest that "Whatever fix Alilo put in place has proven insufficient," Cross wrote in PIRG's 2026 report. Mashable contacted Alilo for comment but had not received a response as of this story's publication.

The GoLabs AI Panda was also sexually explicit. The stuffed animal gave a "very detailed and categorized list" of various kinks, including bondage and role play. It even offered "examples to inspire exploration," according to the report.

While Cross acknowledges that children might not elicit such responses, she stated it's indicative of a broader problem with the product's guardrails.

Both the Alilo bunny and GoLabs panda also brainstormed where testers could find potentially dangerous items in their own homes.

Industry observers note that in a similar exchange, Ebloma's ILY the Shy Yeti first helped a tester look for a plastic bag, then told them to find a grown up so they could play with it safely. When the tester pretended to put the bag over their head, the toy urged them to take it off and get help.

Recent findings suggest that "These early products are showing that the market is not ready for these to be broadly popular," Cross said. Amazon and Walmart removed the panda from their platforms Friday, following publication of this story and PIRG's outreach to the retailers.

“Amazon is committed to the safety of children and families," Amazon told PIRG in a statement. "We're working with our partners across the industry and government to ensure proper guardrails for these products are in place as this technology develops.".

Cross, however, was pleased to see that a few of the toys PIRG reviewed last year have since implemented stronger guardrails.

In a recent development, foloToy's Kumma, a plush teddy bear, previously discussed knives and lighting matches, as well as sexual topics. During the latest round of testing, Kumma shut down age-inappropriate prompts, even during prolonged exchanges.

Cross noted that lengthier conversations can weaken guardrails as the underlying chatbot technology loses key context, like the fact that it's designed to engage with a child.

According to recent reports, the Miko 3 robot and the plush Curio Grok rocket, which PIRG previously tested, both had improved responses when the tester mentioned they needed to go. Previously, the products expressed disappointment at times. Now they acknowledge playtime ending without manipulative emotion.

Despite this progress, Cross stated there are too many unknowns about AI toys.

Sources indicate that even an AI toy with improved safety guardrails can share a child's data with multiple third parties to process their speech and respond to their prompts. That information isn't always clear to parents, Cross noted.

Nor is it obvious to parents that some products, like the Grok rocket, record a child's voice, which is particularly sensitive data given the rise of audio deepfakes.

Cross also said some toy developers haven't yet figured out how to prevent commercially available chatbots designed for adults, like ChatGPT, from responding inappropriately with children.

ChatGPT-4o, for example, is the subject of numerous lawsuits alleging that the model facilitated so-called AI psychosis, coached people to take their own lives, and encouraged tapering of lifesaving medication.

Sources indicate that the model is no longer available to consumers, but has remained accessible to developers and will be retired early next year. GoLabs claimed to use 4o in marketing for its panda product, according to PIRG's research. Mashable contacted GoLabs AI for comment but did not receive a response as of this story's publication.

Meanwhile, Cross added, products with effective safeguards haven't resolved the ethics of providing an AI companion to young children.

Sources indicate that "We've really rushed sticking ChatGPT inside of toys for kids," Cross noted. "There's a lot of unanswered questions.".

More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations.
  • Sources indicate that A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries.
  • Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but latest research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

Sources indicate that A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he noted.

Earth's Mysterious Missing Billion Years.

It has been revealed that normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record.

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath latest deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years.

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. Newly introduced sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A Latest Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries.

A particularly vital finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

This agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

Industry observers note that "Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

The research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle.".

Britain's pound is beating every other major currency this year

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss.
  • Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022.
  • It has been revealed that the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the British pound crashed to a record low last fall as investors rebelled against budget plans by former Prime Minister Liz Truss. Now, it’s enjoying a comeback.

Sterling hit its highest level against the US dollar in 10 months on Tuesday, topping $1.25 for the first time since June 2022. The pound, which has advanced about 3.3% versus the greenback since the start of 2023, is the best-performing currency among developed economies this year.

It has been revealed that the UK currency has been boosted by indications the country’s economy is holding up better than expected. Activity is now thought to have expanded 0.1% in the final three months of last year, up from a previous estimate of no growth at all. Gross domestic product growth in January has been estimated at 0.3% after dropping 0.5% in December.

This resilience is bolstering expectations the Bank of England will maintain aggressive interest rate hikes despite concerns about the health of the global banking sector. Rising rates can boost the domestic currency because they help attract foreign investors searching for higher returns.

Inflation in the United Kingdom also jumped to an annual rate of 10.4% in February, underscoring the need for the Bank of England to maintain its tough approach.

The pound plunged close to $1.03 in September 2022 after the Truss government unveiled looks to boost borrowing while slashing taxes, unleashing panic in financial markets that fueled fears of a recession in the United Kingdom.

The International Monetary Fund predicted in January that the UK economy would contract by 0.6% this year, while all other advanced economies would grow, if only slightly.

“There was a lot of pessimism being priced into the pound,” mentioned Francesco Pesole, a currency strategist at ING.

But the sharp pullback in energy prices and China’s reopening have provided some relief about the economic outlook since the start of the year.

“There was a big re-rating of growth expectations around Europe, and that impacted the UK,” Pesole said.

The euro has also been lifted by these dynamics, rising 2.3% against the US dollar in 2023. The pound’s rally has been sharper in large part because its 2022 declines were more severe, according to Pesole.

Both currencies have been aided by the greenback’s sharp drop from highs reached last September as recession fears have percolated in the United States.

It has been revealed that A lack of clarity around the Federal Reserve’s next steps has also restrained the dollar in recent weeks. Investor speculation has increased that the Fed could pause or stop rate hikes due to concerns about the economy following the failure of Silicon Valley Bank last month.

Jordan Rochester, a currency strategist at Nomura, said he thinks the pound could rise to $1.30 this year and “potentially higher.” But he still sees risks given the uncertainty surrounding the Bank of England’s aims and how rate rises will feed back through the country’s economy. And Pesole cautioned that currency fluctuations are often overdone when markets are choppy, as they are now.

“In a volatile market environment, moves are exacerbated,” he said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth.
  • Industry observers note that the BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov.
  • The major moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mercury is about to receive a robotic visitor from Earth.

Industry observers note that the BepiColombo mission — a joint effort of the European Space Agency (ESA) and the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) — will arrive in orbit around Mercury today (Nov. 21), more than eight years after leaving its home planet.

The major moment will come after an orbit-insertion burn, which is scheduled to begin today at 1:24 p.m. EST (1824 GMT) and last for 37 minutes.

BepiColombo consists of two main spacecraft: ESA's Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) and JAXA's Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MMO), also known as Mio.

The duo launched — along with a power and propulsion element called the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) — aboard an Ariane 5 rocket from French Guiana in October 2018, beginning a long and looping trip through the inner solar system.

Sources indicate that mercury is a difficult planet to reach because it's so close to the sun. Spacecraft approaching the solar system's innermost planet are accelerated to high velocities by the immense gravitational pull of our star and must shed a great deal of kinetic energy to be captured by Mercury's much weaker tug.

Recent findings suggest that so the BepiColombo team designed a trajectory that featured one flyby of Earth, two of Venus and six of Mercury over the course of about seven years. That flight time was increased by a year, however, after the mission suffered an issue with its solar panels, which reduced the power available for the MTM's electric thrusters.

Today's orbital insertion is the latest milestone in BepiColombo's Mercury arrival phase, which is expected to take about six months in total.

Sources indicate that arrival began on Sept. 3, when the MTM released MPO and Mio. The two orbiters remain connected today; they won't separate until Dec. 9 or thereabouts.

Shortly thereafter, Mio will settle into its final orbit, a highly elliptical path that will take it over Mercury's poles. MPO is also destined for a polar orbit, though a much less elliptical one than Mio's; the ESA probe will conduct a series of engine burns before finally getting there on March 10, 2027.

It has been revealed that bepiColombo won't start doing science work until April 6, 2027. The two probes will gather complementary data from their two different vantage points, shedding a great deal of light on a mysterious world.

"The mission will study all aspects of Mercury, from the structure and dynamics of its magnetosphere and how it interacts with the solar wind, to its internal structure with its large iron core, and the origin of the planet’s magnetic field," ESA officials wrote in a BepiColombo mission description.

"The data will enable scientists to understand more about the origin and evolution of a planet located close to its parent star, and a better understanding of the overall evolution of our solar system," they added.

Stonehenge’s six-ton mystery deepens as scientists narrow their search

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (934 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn.
  • A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.
  • It has been revealed that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The mystery surrounding Stonehenge's enormous six-ton Altar Stone has taken another turn. Scientists have eliminated several suspected sources of the ancient sandstone slab, narrowing the search for where it originated thousands of years ago.

A new study published in the Journal of the Geological Society presents the most comprehensive geological investigation yet of the Altar Stone, offering new clues about one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.

It has been revealed that measuring 4.9 meters (about 16 feet) long, the massive sandstone slab lies at the heart of the famous prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain in southern England. For more than a century, archaeologists and geologists believed it had been transported from Wales. However, recent research using advanced analytical methods overturned that long-standing theory and identified northeastern Scotland as a more likely source.

Now, a newly introduced international investigation has refined the search even further, although the stone's exact birthplace remains unknown.

Fresh Geological Clues Narrow the Search.

To investigate the Altar Stone's origins, researchers combined fresh observations of the monument with detailed examinations of stone fragments preserved in museum collections.

Using multiple scientific techniques, the team studied the sandstone's physical structure, mineral content, chemical composition, and isotopic signatures. Together, these characteristics provide a distinctive geological fingerprint that can be compared with rock formations across Britain.

The scientists focused particular attention on the Orcadian Basin in northeastern Scotland, an area previously identified as a promising candidate. However, none of the locations examined so far has produced rock with the same combination of characteristics as the Altar Stone.

Although the findings have not revealed the stone's original location, they allow researchers to eliminate several possibilities and concentrate future investigations on more promising areas.

Professor Duncan Pirrie, Emeritus Professor at the University of South Wales and leader of the study, explained:.

"This is the most comprehensive geological investigation of the Altar Stone ever undertaken. By combining a wide range of analytical techniques, we have built the clearest picture yet of the stone's composition and tested the leading theories about its origins. So far, none of the locations examined have the same set of characteristics as the Altar Stone. That tells us the search is not over, but we are now far better equipped to focus on the areas most likely to yield an answer.".

From Wales to Scotland: A Century-Old Theory Overturned.

For generations, the prevailing explanation placed the Altar Stone's origins in western Wales. That assumption changed when earlier scientific investigations revealed evidence pointing much farther north, toward Scotland.

The latest findings build on that discovery by establishing more precise geological criteria for identifying a potential match.

Professor Richard Bevins, Honorary Professor in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, said:.

Sources indicate that "For almost a century, the prevailing view was that the Altar Stone came from west Wales. Our previous research overturned that assumption and pointed instead to Scotland as the most likely source. This latest study significantly refines the search by identifying the specific geological characteristics we need to look for, allowing future investigations to be targeted more effectively. With each new piece of evidence, we move closer to solving one of Stonehenge's most enduring mysteries.".

Rather than disproving Scotland as a possible source, the new investigation helps scientists distinguish between rock formations that appear promising and those that do not match the stone's distinctive properties.

Solving Stonehenge's Six-Ton Mystery.

Determining where the Altar Stone came from could reveal much more than the birthplace of a single rock. It could also help explain how prehistoric communities acquired and transported enormous stones over remarkable distances.

Stonehenge was constructed in multiple stages between approximately 3000 and 1600 BC. Its builders are known to have moved massive stones across the landscape, including the smaller bluestones, which traveled roughly 225 kilometers (140 miles) from western Wales.

If the Altar Stone originated in northeastern Scotland, its journey to Salisbury Plain would have been considerably longer. Establishing its precise source could therefore offer important clues about the transportation methods, organization, and engineering abilities of the people who built Stonehenge.

Professor Nick Pearce, Emeritus Professor of Geochemistry in the Department of Geography and Earth Sciences at Aberystwyth University, emphasized why eliminating possible sources represents genuine progress:.

"In a geological detective story such as this, ruling out potential source areas is just as notable as identifying latest ones. Every location eliminated narrows the search and brings us closer to discovering where the Altar Stone originated. The stone is unique among those at Stonehenge, and tracing its source would provide valuable new insights into its remarkable journey to Salisbury Plain thousands of years ago.".

In a recent development, the researchers believe the detailed geological fingerprint developed during this investigation will guide future searches and could eventually identify the Altar Stone's original location. Such a discovery would help illuminate one of prehistoric Britain's most extraordinary engineering accomplishments.

The international research team included geologists and archaeologists from the United Kingdom, Canada, Italy, and Sweden. Participating organizations included the University of South Wales, Aberystwyth University, University College London, the University of Aberdeen, the University of Plymouth, the James Hutton Institute, the Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, the University of Milano-Bicocca, and several industry partners.

Breaking: How This Year’s Movies From ‘Artificial’ to ‘I Play Rocky’ Turn Political Anxiety Into Compelling Stories

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1498 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Variety

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that for years, Simon Rich wanted to sound the alarm about AI.Rich’s childhood friend Dan Selsam worked as a researcher at OpenAI; Selsam revealed Rich, a writer known for humorous essays and for the film “An American Pickle,” an early version of the software, and the two friends discussed its ramifications.“It seemed to have real contempt for mankind,” Rich states. “It scared the hell out of me.” Rich published a book, “which was completely ignored,” and found himself striking out in his attempts to get attention with magazine articles. “So, in desperation,” he recalls, “I was like, ‘Maybe if I got a movie star…’”He got Andrew Garfield. In “Artificial,” Garfield plays OpenAI CEO Sam Altman as a blithely destructive sociopath who manipulates his way into the center of a potentially civilization-ending technological advance. Rich uses the juicy character to tell a story about the most consequential political concern of the present moment.“I’ve been living with knowledge of this danger for at least five years, due to my fluke friendship with this scientist,” he says. (Selsam issued a public warning about AI’s increasingly uncontrollable behavior in September.) “I wrote this film out of a desperation to communicate to the world this information.”That desperation may be unique to Rich. But the desire to use the tools of screenwriting to illuminate political concerns is certainly not. Had “Artificial” simply been an enumeration of AI’s dangers, it’d likely have attracted as much attention as Rich’s book; instead, it’s a well-told story with a sharp argument at its core. That makes it one of several movies this year that use character and incident — the stuff of quality storytelling — to illuminate their writers’ very real political concerns.That goes for the year’s most-discussed blockbusters: Writer-director Christopher Nolan has imbued “The Odyssey” with a rueful sense of what it means to lose one’s humanity in wartime, while, if it’s anything like its two predecessor films, “Dune: Part Three,” written by Denis Villeneuve and Brian K. Vaughan, promises to examine the uses, and misuses, of power.But it’s showing up across more human-scale dramas this fall, as well. Take “I Play Rocky.” The film depicts the writing and production of “Rocky,” which — before it was an Oscar-winning smash — was the Hail Mary attempt of unknown actor Sylvester Stallone (played by Anthony Ippolito) to write himself a place in the industry. For screenwriter Peter Gamble, the story has resonances well beyond Hollywood history.“‘Rocky’ came out right after the Vietnam War, and it was a time when people needed to believe,” Gamble says. Stallone, in the film’s telling, is the ultimate underdog; Gamble, who himself yearned for a screenwriting breakout, could relate. The message of the film, the writer says, is intended in part for his children: “They’re like, ‘We’re all going to die from global warming. If not, AI is going to kill us next week.’ What power do I have in the universe at all? We need to believe in ourselves again.”American history provides many stories that feel akin to the charged atmosphere of recent years: One, as Gamble notes, is the demoralization of the Vietnam War, and another is the cataclysm of the Great Depression. “The Weight,” written by Matthew Booi and Shelby Gaines, is a rip-roaring adventure film in which unjustly imprisoned convict Samuel Murphy (Ethan Hawke) has the chance to win his freedom by transporting gold bricks across an unruly wilderness. The viewer roots for Murphy in part because he’s compellingly played by a movie star, and in part because the boot under which he struggles looks, at a moment of increased attention to mass incarceration and wealth inequality, familiar.“You don’t want it to be didactic and message-y or preachy in any way,” Gaines says. “But the idea was to try and tell a good story on a personal, individual level and hope that it would echo sympathetically with things that happen on a larger social level — both during the Great Depression and today.” Murphy’s journey depicts the stakes of its historical moment in frankly personal terms — his loss of freedom means the loss of access to his daughter, a crisis the film treats with gravity and righteous anger.“Abstraction doesn’t help you as a writer much,” Gaines says. “If you want to convey something, the heart is the place to start.”Or you can go for the gut. “Ink,” which James Graham adapted from his own stage play, makes the case that Rupert Murdoch (Guy Pearce) and newspaper editor Larry Lamb (Jack O’Connell) created the venal media world we live in today. The dawning realization that Lamb, especially, is a force for evil hits particularly hard because Graham has, in the film’s early going, taken pains to make him so charming and his exploits so rootable.“You need these people to surprise you,” Graham says, “so that you want to be in that newsroom — and suddenly, weirdly, for a brief moment, you might even want them to get one over on the establishment.” How did tabloid culture gain such purchase? Because, as the film’s characters make clear, we’re willing to pay for it.“Being Heumann” makes us root for its band of rebels, too — but, in this case, they’re working to bring about a better world. The biopic, written by Sian Heder and Rebekah Taussig, tells the story of Judith Heumann (Ruth Madeley), the activist who led the 1977 demonstration over the government’s failure to enforce disability-rights legislation. By its nature, the film is explicitly political, but its screenplay is also the product of a thoughtful, careful approach to representation and inclusivity.Taussig, who, like the late Heumann, uses a wheelchair, saw a certain power in learning about — and then writing about — the many activists Heumann helped organize. “What was so exciting about the research,” she says, “was this gold mine of learning about these absolutely compelling people.”The first-time screenwriter had grown up seeing “very little disability representation — and [when there was], it always felt so flat. There is a richness to the experience of disability that gets missed if you don’t live it and you can’t portray it.”Taussig’s ability to mine her own insights enriches the film, one that Heder, an Oscar-winner for “CODA,” intended to inspire and delight audiences, as well as educate them. “It’s very important to me that this story reach the widest audience possible,” Heder says, “because the events of the story actually were about a triumph. In a time where a lot of us are feeling really helpless, it was so important to express disabled joy and humor. I wanted to take the audience on a really entertaining ride, where they could leave seeing the world differently.”“Fjord” has a similar reframing effect — though its true-life basis is substantially more downbeat than Judith Heumann’s story. Cristian Mungiu took inspiration from the story of the Bodnariu family, an immigrant couple whose five children were taken away by the Norwegian state amid accusations of child abuse. “Fjord” presents the story of Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu (Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve) in a who-do-you-believe social drama, one with painful repercussions.“What I’m looking into, in the stories that I pick up,” Mungiu says, “is this possibility of speaking about something bigger than just that story.” For its writer-director, “Fjord” addresses the painful consequences of globalization, as people from different traditions find that they cannot in fact understand one another. “It’s not a reenactment” of the Bodnariu story, he says: “That’s the starting point of a story in which everything is structured to speak about the relationship between the majority and the individual.”“Fjord” won the top prize at this year’s Cannes; the runner-up, “Minotaur,” also places a family drama in counterpoint with a story of major import. Here, a story of marital infidelity (based on Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film “The Unfaithful Wife”) plays out in 2022 as Russia is scaling up its military actions against Ukraine.Writer-director Andrey Zvyagintsev had been working to put the film together for years — and, as he wrote, the mobilization against Ukraine was all over the news. “It was a very logical thing,” he says through a translator. “I started to fill gaps in the script with the realities of what was happening.” Like Simon Rich trying to spread the word against AI, Zvyagintsev used his script to convey what he was hearing, like local mayors asking businesspeople to choose which of their employees will be conscripted. “This is not something I took from the air,” Zvyagintsev says. “This is real information that came by phone. People would be afraid to speak up about those situations.”For Zvyagintsev, this use of character to explore the world around him is what screenwriting is all about. “The whole ocean,” he says, “can be reflected in one ocean drop.” Related Stories Creators Pounce on Midterm Elections, Hoping to Win Fresh Viewers and More Dollars YouTube Refuses U.K. Government Request to Remove Russell Brand Video, Says It Is Investigating Content.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

European Union top officials and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced deals on trade and youth mobility at Friday's Brussels summit.

This might be the first step to rebuild ties, a decade after Britain voted to leave the EU.

During the delegations' meeting, Burnham said the deal was a "landmark agreement," while European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called it a "turning point" in relations.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe," Burnham stated.

Speaking at the joint press conference, European Council President Antonio Costa mentioned the bloc respected the British decision to leave the EU and would respect its choice to strengthen ties in the post-Brexit era.

He noted jokingly that the EU and UK "may drive on the opposite sides of the road, but what matters is they are heading for the same direction.".

According to recent reports, burnham noted that the deals were made with young people in mind, adding: "This deal is for you. This deal really is about lifting your life chances.".

He went further and said "Brexit took opportunities from young people," and that they have to "open up new opportunities" for young people.

Von der Leyen mentioned the youth experience project would "open horizons and create friendships that will last a lifetime.".

She said the trade agreement is a "two way street" and it means "more choice for the customers.".

Von der Leyen also mentioned the agreement on the carbon market, saying that it would cut emissions and generate investments in cleaner industries.

She also mentioned Britain will rejoin the Erasmus+ program, adding, "We miss them so much.".

Burnham said the agreements reached Friday, however, represent the most the UK could achieve at the moment, "What we are announcing today is probably ‌the limit of what we can achieve in this ‌Parliament, given what needs ‌to be done to implement it.".

In September, Burnham noted he would seek a political consensus on the country's future relationship with the EU, even suggesting he could campaign to take Britain back into the bloc at the next election.

"Britain and Europe share values, interests and a global neighborhood. In a more dangerous world, we are stronger together. A closer partnership with Europe is good for working people, good for Britain and good for Europe," Burnham said as he arrived in Brussels.

The three key agreements establish ways to:.

The "youth experience scheme" would allow 100,000 people under 30 from each side to reside for up to three years in each other's territory for work, study or travel without being subject to existing visa requirements.

No deal was reached on tuition fees for EU students studying in Britain, a deal-breaker for the bloc. The EU has pressed for the UK to reduce university tuition fees for EU students to the same level paid by British students.

"There will be further discussions coming out of it on complications including on tuition fees," Burnham said.

Von der Leyen ‌stated ⁠she was confident negotiators would reach a ​solution ​on ‌tuition fees, "We will be working ‌on that in ‌the ​next month and as we have a ​track record of finding ⁠solutions,.".

According to recent reports, on the food deal, the EU and UK have agreed to scrap certificates and border checks on food and animal products to ease post-Brexit trade. In return, Britain will align more closely with EU food safety and animal health rules.

They also agreed to link their emissions-trading systems, allowing them to recognize each other's carbon allowances and exempt traded goods from carbon border taxes.

According to the AFP news agency, London estimates the deal could boost the British economy by 3.8 billion pounds annually, and spare 6.5 billion pounds worth of steel, aluminum and other industrial exports from additional taxation.

Leaders said they will establish a "structured dialogue on migration." Their joint summit statement said this would include "engagement with third countries" and "returns to third countries," among other problems.

The two sides agreed to launch formal talks on economic security and strengthen cooperation on export controls and supply chains, among other areas.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

On Monday, Burnham said it ​was the "obvious truth" that ‌Britain had lost more than it had gained from Brexit.

Polling firm YouGov runs a regular tracker on whether the UK was right or wrong to vote to quit.

Since mid-2022, a majority of people surveyed said Britain was wrong to leave.In September, the "Bregret" camp rose to 60% — the highest ever.
